knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function

$$
f=7 \sin{\left(u \right)}, \qquad u=12 x + 6.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}u}=7 \cos{\left(u \right)},\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=12.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}u}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}\\&=(7 \cos{\left(u \right)})\cdot(12)\\&=84 \cos{\left(u \right)}\\&=84 \cos{\left(12 x + 6 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as a composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{tan}⁡u,\,u=14{x}^{4}-10.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\sec^{2}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=56{x}^{3}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\sec^{2}⁡u\cdot 56{x}^{3} \\  & =56{x}^{3}\sec^{2}⁡u \\  & =56{x}^{3}\sec^{2}⁡(14{x}^{4}-10).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (34x + 11).

$$
\begin{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}

& =45\pi \cos(26\pi) \\
&= 45\pi \cdot (1) \\
&= 45\pi
\end{aligned}

$$

\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (18x + 22).

\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$


Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is 
$$
m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-40\pi}.
$$
